growth.juvenile_note: Starts as a small rosette of soft, grey-silky, oblong leaves with a few shallow teeth; within weeks it sends out sprawling, hairy stems that lie along the sand with upturned tips, making a low grey-green mound. Large lemon-yellow flowers open at dusk and wilt orange by midday; the stems catch blowing sand, so the plant rides up with the dune.
growth.source: Estimated from Flora of North America (O. drummondii: annual or short-lived perennial of Gulf coast dunes, decumbent grey-strigose stems, yellow vespertine flowers) and invasive-range reports (flowers within its first season, spreads along coastal dunes)

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings come up in spring on bare foredune sand as a single narrow grass shoot with thin, rolled leaves and deep roots. By the end of the first season it is a small tuft; in the second it tillers heavily and sends rhizomes 0.6-1.8 m a year, new shoots pushing up through blown sand. The tall arching culms with flat golden spikelets come later.
growth.source: USDA FEIS (Uniola paniculata): 30 days cold-moist at 4 C then 78-89% germination at alternating temperatures; seedlings establish in the first season and tiller extensively by the second; lateral spread 0.6-1.8 m a year; sand burial stimulates growth; flowers Jun-Nov; about 30% of ovaries set seed. Wikipedia: 1-2 m. First flowering and clump lifespan estimated.

Established plants run a long straight rhizome just under the sand, sending up a small leafy shoot every few nodes, so the plant shows as neat straight lines of short tufts marching across dunes.

canopy.name: Stone pine

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings have 10-13 cotyledons and for 5-10 years carry juvenile foliage: single, soft, silvery blue-green needles 2-4 cm long, making a bushy, rounded, bluish globe rather than a cone. Adult paired, stiff green needles gradually take over by about age 10; the tree then lifts into a flat umbrella crown on a bare trunk.
growth.source: Wikipedia (juvenile leaves for 5-10 years, fully adult by ~10; a bushy globe in youth, an umbrella in mid-age; 12-20 m typical, to 25+; cones take 36 months to mature, longest of any pine); first cones and lifespan estimated

canopy.source: Mediterranean coasts; 15–25 m. Umbrella crown; pine nuts. Kew POWO for the name; standard floras for range.

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with 3-6 cotyledons and a tuft of single primary needles, then short, twisted, paired needles. Young trees are dense, narrow cones with regular whorls. Open-grown shore pines become bushy, crooked and flat-topped; inland trees become slim, straight poles. Serotinous cones stay closed on the branches for decades.
growth.source: USDA Silvics (Lotan & Critchfield): viable seed commonly at 5-10 years; ~3.6 m at 20 years on medium sites; germination peaks in the 2 weeks after snowmelt; very intolerant of shade; shore pine small and short-lived; ages commonly 150-200+, old high-elevation trees to 400+

fruiting.source: USDA Silvics (reddish-purple female strobili in whorls of 2-5, mid-May to mid-July; cones mature Aug-Oct over a year after pollination, purple-green to light brown; Rocky Mountain cones serotinous, sealed until heated to 45-60 C and held for years; 10-24 seeds per cone)

It branches low into a stiff, rounded, grey-twigged bush and sends up root suckers, so on dunes and old fields single plants become dense, flat-topped colonies; root nodules fix nitrogen in poor sand.
growth.source: Wikipedia (to 4.5 m; catkins 3-18 mm, green to red; fruit 3-5.5 mm with pale blue-purple wax, key winter food of yellow-rumped warblers; nitrogen-fixing nodules); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Myrica (2-8 ft shrub; waxy drupes persist over winter); ages estimated

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (catkins 3-18 mm, green to red; fruit 3-5.5 mm with a pale blue-grey waxy coat, eaten through winter by yellow-rumped warblers and tree swallows); USDA Woody Plant Seed Manual Myrica (mostly dioecious, dry waxy drupes persisting over winter); wind pollination; months, set and crop estimated

Growth rate estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: two cotyledons, then feathery bipinnate juvenile leaves (like a tiny fern frond) for the first season or two, gradually replaced by long, flat, bright-green phyllodes with 2-4 parallel veins. Young plants are fast, bushy, many-branched shrubs that flower by year 2-3. Mass germination follows fire.
